ai.literal: Having stayed, having protected, home-living all, guest having cherished, service doing for the sake of.
ai.translation: Staying at home and protecting one's resources is entirely for the sake of cherishing guests and doing them service.
ai.modern: வீட்டில் இருந்து பொருள்களைக் காத்து வாழும் இல்லற வாழ்க்கை எல்லாம், விருந்தினரை உபசரித்து அவர்களுக்கு உதவி செய்வதற்காகவே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the primary purpose of domestic life. Staying at home and preserving one's resources is not for selfish enjoyment. Rather, the entirety of family life is meant for welcoming guests and offering them hospitable service. The word 'vēḷāṇmai' here specifically means helpful service or hospitality, rather than its other common meaning of agriculture.

ai.literal: guest being outside oneself eating non-dying medicine even if desirable nature it is not.
ai.translation: Even if it is the medicine of immortality, eating it all by oneself while a guest waits outside is not to be desired.
ai.modern: விருந்தினர் வீட்டின் வெளியே காத்திருக்க, சாவாமையைத் தரும் அமிழ்தமே ஆனாலும் அதனைத் தான் மட்டும் உண்பது விரும்பத்தக்கது அன்று.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme importance of hospitality in classical Tamil culture. The phrase 'சாவா மருந்து' refers to a medicine that prevents death, often understood as the nectar of immortality. The poet declares that even if one possesses such a miraculous substance, consuming it alone while a guest remains unfed outside is entirely undesirable. The words 'தான் உண்டல்' (eating by oneself) contrast sharply with the communal and generous spirit expected of a householder.

ai.literal: Coming guests every day he who cares for life having suffered falling into ruin is not.
ai.translation: The life of one who cares for arriving guests every day will never suffer and fall into ruin.
ai.modern: நாள்தோறும் வரும் விருந்தினர்களைப் போற்றி உபசரிப்பவனின் வாழ்க்கை, துன்பப்பட்டுப் பாழாவது இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the continuous practice of hospitality. The phrase 'வருவிருந்து வைகலும் ஓம்புவான்' describes a householder who welcomes and cares for guests every single day. The word 'பருவந்து' means experiencing distress or suffering. The couplet assures that such a generous person's domestic life will never face the sorrow of falling into ruin.

ai.literal: Heart being pleased, Prosperity will dwell, face being pleased, good guests he who cherishes' house.
ai.translation: Prosperity will dwell with a joyful heart in the home of one who cherishes good guests with a welcoming face.
ai.modern: முகம் மலர்ந்து நல்ல விருந்தினரை உபசரிப்பவனின் வீட்டில் செல்வம் மனம் மகிழ்ந்து தங்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the reward of welcoming guests warmly. The word 'செய்யாள்' literally means a red-hued woman, representing Prosperity or Wealth. Just as the host welcomes guests with a pleased and smiling face ('முகன் அமர்ந்து'), Prosperity herself will be pleased in her heart ('அகன் அமர்ந்து') to take up permanent residence in that host's home.

ai.literal: Even seed sowing is needed indeed? - guest having cherished, remainder he who eats - [his] field.
ai.translation: Is it even necessary to sow seeds in the field of a man who eats only what remains after feeding his guests?
ai.modern: விருந்தினரை உபசரித்து உணவளித்த பின் எஞ்சியதை உண்பவனுடைய நிலத்தில் விதைகளை விதைக்கவும் வேண்டுமா?
ai.explanation: This couplet asks a rhetorical question about the prosperity of a generous host. The phrase 'விருந்து ஓம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான்' describes a person who first feeds their guests and only eats the leftovers. The poet wonders if such a person even needs to sow seeds ('வித்தும் இடல் வேண்டும் கொல்லோ') in their field ('புலம்'). The implication is that nature itself will reward their hospitality, making their land yield abundantly without effort. The word 'கொல்லோ' emphasizes the rhetorical nature of the question, highlighting the supreme value of cherishing guests.

ai.literal: Departing guest having cared for, coming guest having looked for he who will be, good guest to the heavenly beings.
ai.translation: He who cares for the departing guest and waits for the coming guest will be a welcome guest to the heavenly beings.
ai.modern: சென்ற விருந்தினரை உபசரித்து வழியனுப்பிவிட்டு, இனி வரும் விருந்தினரை எதிர்பார்த்திருப்பவன், வானுலகத்தில் உள்ள தேவர்களுக்கும் நல்ல விருந்தினன் ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the continuous nature of true hospitality. A virtuous householder does not stop at serving one guest; after warmly sending off a departing guest, they immediately look forward to welcoming the next. Such a person, who makes hospitality their life's constant practice, will themselves be welcomed as an honored guest by the celestial beings in heaven. The word 'வருந்து' in the provided text functions as a variant of 'விருந்து', meaning guest.

ai.literal: "Of this measure" that which is said one thing is not; of the guest measure-measure sacrifice's fruit.
ai.translation: The benefit of the sacrifice of hospitality cannot be quantified as being "just this much". Its measure is exactly commensurate with the worth of the guests.
ai.modern: விருந்தோம்பல் என்னும் வேள்வியின் பயன் இவ்வளவுதான் என்று அளவிட்டுக் கூற முடியாது. அது வந்த விருந்தினரின் தகுதிக்கு ஏற்ற அளவினைக் கொண்டதாகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet compares the act of hosting guests to a sacred sacrifice ('வேள்வி'). It states that the spiritual or moral benefit ('பயன்') of this hospitality cannot be restricted to a specific, quantifiable amount ('இனைத்துணைத்து'). Instead, the reward is directly proportional to the worth and quality of the guests ('விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை'). Thus, the true value of hospitality lies in the merit of those who are welcomed.

ai.literal: Having toiled, having hoarded, 'support we are without' they will say, guests having cherished, the sacrifice those who do not undertake.
ai.translation: Those who do not undertake the sacrifice of cherishing guests will later lament, 'We toiled and hoarded, but now we are without support.'
ai.modern: விருந்தினரை உபசரிக்கும் வேள்வியை செய்யாதவர்கள், பொருளை வருந்தி பாதுகாத்தும் இப்போது எந்தப் பற்றும் இல்லாமல் போனோம் என்று வருந்துவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns about the regret of those who hoard wealth without sharing it. The word 'parintu' means toiling or guarding with anxious care, emphasizing the selfish effort spent on hoarding. The poet uses 'velvi' (sacrifice) to show that hospitality is as sacred and essential as a formal ritual. Those who fail to undertake this duty will eventually realize that their hoarded wealth offers no real support, lamenting that they are left destitute of true companionship.

ai.literal: Within wealth poverty guest-cherishing not-practicing stupidity; ignorant people-with exists.
ai.translation: The poverty within wealth is the stupidity of failing to cherish guests. Such stupidity is found only among the ignorant.
ai.modern: செல்வம் இருந்தும் வறுமையாக இருப்பது விருந்தினரை உபசரிக்காத அறியாமையாகும். அந்த அறியாமை அறிவற்றவர்களிடம் மட்டுமே இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts material wealth with the moral poverty of not hosting guests. The word inmai can mean non-existence or poverty; here it means poverty, directly contrasting with udaimai (wealth) to show that riches are useless if unshared. The word ompa means failing to protect or cherish, which defines the madamai or stupidity of the wealthy miser. Ultimately, the poet states that this specific kind of stupidity exists only among madavar, the truly ignorant.

ai.literal: Upon smelling will wither the aniccam; face having changed upon looking will wither the guest.
ai.translation: The delicate aniccam flower withers just by being smelled. A guest withers when looked at with a changed face.
ai.modern: மோந்து பார்த்தாலே அனிச்ச மலர் வாடிவிடும். அதுபோல, முகம் சுளித்து வேறுபட்டுப் பார்த்தாலே வந்த விருந்தினர் உள்ளம் வாடிவிடுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the extreme sensitivity of guests by comparing them to the delicate aniccam flower. The flower droops simply from the breath of someone smelling it. Similarly, a guest's heart will wither the moment a host looks at them with a changed or unwelcoming expression. The parallel between smelling and looking emphasizes that even the slightest hint of displeasure is enough to hurt a guest, highlighting the need for a genuinely cheerful welcome.
